1:
The first thing noted is that nothing begins here. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) calls the division of the chapters unfortunate, there being no break in the story, and takes the prophet to be addressing the king and the attendants present. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes the word a reply to the desponding language of the king at the close of the preceding chapter, vindicating the prophet from the charge of having caused the calamity. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the timing into a rule: the king despaired and grew weary of waiting, and then Elisha foretold it, when things were at the worst, for man’s extremity is God’s opportunity of magnifying his power, and his time to appear for his people is when their strength is gone. Though the king had just threatened the prophet’s life, God promises to save it, and his people with him, for where sin abounded grace doth much more abound.

On the measure and the price three voices reckon and agree. Clarke makes the seah about two gallons and a half, and the shekel two shillings and fourpence at the lowest computation, remarking on the wide difference between this and the price of the ass’s head named before. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives it as six cabs, or about a peck and pottle of our measure, the same amount by another road. Ellicott calls the seah the most usual corn measure, and insists the prophet’s words are far more abrupt in the original: thus hath Jehovah said, about this time to-morrow a seah fine flour at a shekel, and two seahs barley at a shekel, in the gate of Samaria. He adds, against Thenius, that the barley was meant not only as fodder but for human food, as barley cakes, and explains the gate by trade, the corn market being held just within it.

The scoffer’s office and posture are settled before his words are weighed. Clarke says the Hebrew term occurs often as the name of an office and seems to point out one of the highest in the state; Ellicott renders it adjutant, or aide-de-camp, or esquire, and compares the phrase about the hand leaned upon with the expression used of Naaman. John Gill (reformed) insists the leaning was not figurative, not merely that the king confided in him, but literal, the king resting on his hand and being supported by him as a form and matter of state. He adds that the title marks a principal lord, the third to the king; that the word the Septuagint uses is interpreted by Suidas of those holding three spears together; and that the like state was kept by the king of Syria and by the kings and queens of Persia.

Whether his death was a judgement is the real disagreement here. Henry calls it the just doom of his infidelity, that he should see the plenty for his conviction and yet not eat of it to his comfort, unbelief being a sin by which men dishonour God and deprive themselves of the favours he designed for them; as the murmuring Israelites saw Canaan and could not enter in, so, says Henry after bishop Patrick, will it be with those who believe not the promise of eternal life: they shall see it at a distance but never taste it. Clarke will not have it so: this was a mere prediction of the man’s death, not a judgment for his unbelief, since any person in his circumstances might have spoken as he did, and any person in his place might have been trodden to death in the gate. What the scoffer said, Clarke grants, was that nothing but a miracle could procure such plenty, and by a miracle alone was it done. Ellicott notices that the answer is shaped to the question, Elisha partly imitating the scoffer’s own words.
3:
One tradition about the lepers is reported at four temperatures. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) passes it on flatly, that the Gemara in Sota and Jarchi and others say these four were Gehazi and his three sons, adding that at the entering in of the gate means they were not suffered to mingle in society. John Gill (reformed) reports the same tradition and explains the place: lepers being obliged by law to be outside the city and camp, these may have had a dwelling assigned near the gate, or got as near as they could, partly for relief, partly for fear of the Syrians. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) half accepts it, that perhaps Gehazi was one, which might be why the king noticed him later; and he makes the exclusion providential, Samaria being delivered and not knowing it, so that four men shut out as unclean became its intelligencers. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) will have none of it, noting the ascription to Rashi with an exclamation and nothing more, and explaining their plight without it: nobody brought them food any longer, owing to the famine.

Their reasoning is drawn out by Henry, pared back by Ellicott. Henry lays the options side by side: go into the city, and there was nothing to be had, they must die in the streets; sit still, and they must pine to death in their cottage; so they determined to throw themselves on the enemy’s mercy, better dying by the sword than by famine, one death than a thousand. Common prudence, he says, puts us upon the method that may better our condition but cannot make it worse. Ellicott keeps to the words: to fall unto is to desert; if they save us alive means and give us food, for pity’s sake; and the qualifying but is absent from the Hebrew.

Whether the kings the Syrians feared were real or a fantasy is the sharpest division. Henry treats the names as self-deception: as the Syrians were imposed upon by the sound, so they imposed upon themselves by the interpretation of it, for there was for aught we know but one king of Egypt, and what kings there were of the Hittites nobody can imagine. Ellicott answers with history: the tract of north Syria between the Euphrates and the Orontes was the cradle of the Hittite race, over which these kings of the several tribes bore sway, their power once reaching over much of Asia Minor, as inscriptions prove. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes a third way, that under the name of the Hittites, as elsewhere under that of the Amorites, all the people of Canaan are meant, many spared or fled on Joshua’s coming to the bordering lands, where they grew powerful. On the noise itself Gill offers three possibilities: that it was made in the air by angels, or that the Lord so wrought on their imagination that they fancied they heard it, or that he caused the noise in their ears.

The plunder and the change of mind are conscience to two, idiom to one. Henry has them feast in the first tent and begin to think of enriching themselves, until they correct themselves: they do not well to conceal good tidings from the community they belong to, under colour of being avenged for their exclusion, since the law did that and not the people. Selfish people cannot prosper, he adds; and the news was not the less acceptable for being first brought by lepers. Gill puts the scruple plainly: it was not right to take the booty to themselves, not just to their brethren, and might not prove well to themselves in the issue. Ellicott explains the burying as a common practice of Orientals, with whom holes in the ground or the wall serve for banks; and he renders their fear literally: guilt will find us.
12:
The king’s suspicion is excused by two voices, diagnosed by a third. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls the conclusion a very natural one, and credits the man with a noble defence, sharing the sufferings of the besieged and ever at his post: even in vile Ahab there were some good things. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) quotes Grotius, that misery is suspicious, and allows that stratagems such as this king suspected are common in warfare. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) grants the facts and turns them inward: the king knew he had no reason to expect God should appear thus wonderfully for him, having forfeited his favour by unbelief and impatience, and knew no reason the Syrians had to fly, since neither he nor any attendant seems to have heard the noise that frightened them. A guilty conscience, Henry adds, fears the worst and makes men suspicious.

The servant’s speech about the horses is among the hardest verses here, and three voices treat it three ways. Clarke calls it very difficult and follows Kennicott in judging seven Hebrew words a careless scribal repetition, improperly continued in the text: they are absent from the Septuagint and the Syriac, wanting in more than forty manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, unpointed in some, written in and afterwards blotted out in others; and the verse should be read without them. He also renders the last words not consumed but perfect, that is fit for service. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) emends nothing, taking the Hebrew prefix not as a note of similitude but as an affirmation of certainty: behold, they are of a truth all the multitude of the horses of Israel left. The verse deserved its double behold, he says, to show what the famine had done to men and beasts alike, and to what a low ebb the king was come, whose troops of horses had shrunk to so few.

Ellicott keeps the text too, reading the difficulty as pathos rather than corruption. The repetition, he says, dwells pathetically on the fewness of the survivors; and the adviser supposes two contingencies: the horses and their drivers may return safe and share the fortune of all the multitude of Israel that are left, or be taken and slain and so be even as all the multitude that are consumed. The servant is no more sanguine than his master: they must perish in any case, and whether here by famine or there by the sword makes little difference. But he allows that Reuss may be right in finding no fatalism here, only a natural doubt whether starving animals are adequate to the service required, consumed then meaning spent or exhausted.

Why two horses were sent when five were asked divides them again. Henry says it should seem there were only two fit to be sent, and those chariot-horses; John Gill (reformed) agrees and improves it, that they were the best, perhaps those that drew the king’s own chariot, and so better fed and fitter for the journey; Clarke supposes they found on examination that only two were effective. Ellicott denies the premise, taking five as an indefinite small number, like our half a dozen, and reading the Hebrew as teams for two chariots, sent so that if attacked they might make a better resistance, or so that if one were captured the other might escape with the news. On how far the scouts went he parts from Gill as well: Gill has them go as far as Jordan, over which the Syrians must pass, while Ellicott says not to the river itself, at least twenty miles off, but in the direction of it. Of the litter on the road Clarke says it is manifest proof of the hurry and precipitancy of the flight, Henry that the Syrians could be tracked by the garments they threw off for speed.
16:
The plenty itself is passed over quickly. John Gill (reformed) says the people spoiled the tents of their riches and their provisions, of which there was such plenty that it served not only for present use but for sale, which is how the price came down as the prophet had said. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) corrects only the word, that what was spoiled was the camp rather than the tents.

What the gate-keeping commission was for draws three answers. Gill says it was not to keep out an enemy, of which there was now no danger, but to prevent disorders and tumults among the people, that they might go out in an orderly and regular manner. Ellicott agrees and sharpens the picture, that he was to maintain order as the famished crowd poured out of the city, and he reads the verb as a pluperfect: now the king had appointed him. He adds that Reuss takes the charge of the gate to be the charge of the market, the market being held on the space adjoining the gate. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supplies the mechanics of the death from the same commission: the people rushing out to get spoil and in again to carry it to their houses, the officer set over the gate was borne down by the multitude and trodden to death.

On the manner of it Ellicott follows Thenius in a detail that makes it worse: the trampling probably happened as the crowd was returning from the Syrian camp, wild with excess of food and drink after their long abstinence, and the man was trampled down while trying to discharge his duty, so that he saw the plenty with his eyes and did not eat thereof. Clarke draws the moral from the accuracy rather than the horror, that this too was foreseen by the spirit of prophecy, and that the literal and exact fulfilment of such predictions must have acquired the prophet a great deal of credit in Israel; he also sets the whole episode in Lightfoot’s reckoning of the reign, in the fifth year of Jehoram, when Samaria was besieged by Ben-hadad and after being nearly destroyed by famine was suddenly relieved.

That the closing verses repeat what has already been said is treated as deliberate. Gill says the words spoken to the king and to the lord are set down again so that it might be observed how exactly the prophecies were fulfilled. Ellicott puts it more warmly, that the author repeats the prediction and its fulfilment with obvious satisfaction, and that the moral is a warning against unbelief; though he suspects the text has suffered in the process, the phrase who spake being probably a spurious repetition, wanting in some Hebrew manuscripts and in the Syriac and the Vulgate and the Arabic. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) states the warning itself: see how heinously God resents our distrust of his power, providence and promise, for whenever God promises the end, he knows where to provide the means.
